hallucination: When a language model states something false as if it were a fact, like a quote nobody said or a book that was never written.
cutoff date: The day a model’s training data ends. It has seen nothing that happened after it.
biased: A biased model works clearly worse for some groups than for others, usually because of what was (and wasn’t) in its training data. Not the same thing as a neuron’s bias.
accuracy: The share of answers a model got right. Handy, but one accuracy number can hide who the model fails, and it means little when the thing you are looking for is rare.
threshold: The line a score has to reach before the model’s answer counts as a yes. Moving it trades one kind of mistake for another.
false alarm: The model said yes and the truth was no. Also called a false positive.
recall: Of all the real yeses, the share the model caught. Missing a real one lowers it.
precision: Of everything the model flagged as a yes, the share that really was one. False alarms lower it.
shortcut learning: When a model learns an easy pattern that happens to go along with the right answer in its training data, instead of the real reason for the answer.
